sections.title: Emergency systems — the life-safety tier
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 700 covers backup power that the law classes as emergency: power for getting people out and keeping them alive, such as egress lighting, exit signs, fire alarm and similar life-safety loads. A governmental agency having jurisdiction decides that a system is emergency; the owner does not get to choose the label. Emergency power has to be there fast, the wiring is kept apart from normal wiring, and the system is tested and documented. If life safety does not depend on it, you are probably in Article 701 or 702 instead.

• 700.11: New 700.11 sets wiring rules for emergency lighting run on Class 2 power: mark it, keep it apart from other Class 2 cabling, and protect it from damage. Emergency Class 2 wiring now needs physical protection: raceway, cable tray, Type MC or Type AC cable (700.11(D)).
• 700.24: Only luminaires that go into emergency mode because an outside control signal tells them to must be emergency listed. A standard fixture fed through a listed emergency control device doesn't. A luminaire that responds to an outside control input and goes to emergency mode when normal power fails must be listed for emergency use.
• 700.27: New 700.27: a device that feeds Class 2 emergency lighting with both power and control, like a PoE switch, has to carry an emergency lighting control device listing. A device sending Class 2 power and control signals together to emergency lighting must be listed for that job, as an emergency lighting control device.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

sections.title: Tests and maintenance — emergency systems
sections.plain_explanation:
An emergency system is not finished when it is wired. 700.3 builds testing and maintenance into the installation itself:
• (A) Acceptance testing: the AHJ conducts or witnesses a test of the complete system when the installation is finished, and periodically afterward.
• (B) Periodic testing: the system is tested periodically on a schedule the AHJ approves, so it stays in proper operating condition.
• (C) Battery systems: where battery systems or unit equipment are involved, periodic maintenance is required.
• (D) Written record: a written record of the tests and maintenance has to be kept.
• (E) Testing under load: means has to be provided to test the system under its maximum anticipated load.
The manufacturer instructions and industry standards fill in the details of how the equipment is maintained, but the NEC rule the inspector enforces is simple: test it, maintain it, and prove it on paper.
sections.on_the_job: At turnover on a Lake Nona outpatient clinic, Sharma left the owner a test binder, not just keys: the results of the AHJ-witnessed acceptance test, the periodic test schedule the AHJ approved, and the battery maintenance log with the first entries filled in. When the inspector asked how the system would be proven a year later, the answer was the binder — dates, loads, and signatures — not a promise that somebody would get around to it.

nec2023_change.change: Commissioning of the emergency system now has to be done or witnessed by the AHJ, and the hookup point for a temporary generator must be outdoors and fully labeled. The AHJ (authority having jurisdiction) has to commission the whole emergency system, or witness it, at startup and periodically after that (700.3(A)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 700.3 Emergency system commissioning

sections.why_it_exists: Emergency gear sits idle for months and is expected to work perfectly in the first seconds of the worst day. Batteries sulfate, fuel goes stale, transfer switches stick, and a system that is never tested under load fails silently: nobody finds out until the lights are already out and people are on the stairs. Scheduled testing with a written record is what turns a dormant installation into a proven system.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that testing is a one-time event the contractor performs alone at startup and reports afterward. 700.3(A) puts the AHJ in the acceptance test, conducting it or witnessing it, and (B) keeps the testing going on a schedule the AHJ approves. A system with no periodic testing and no written record is not a finished emergency system, however neatly it was wired.

sections.title: Capacity and rating — emergency systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Emergency equipment has to be suitable for the fault current available where it connects — gear that cannot safely carry or interrupt the fault it may see does not belong on a life-safety system. The system also has to have enough capacity for its emergency load, figured under Article 220 or by another method the AHJ approves.
• Capacity means every emergency load that operates at the same time, carried together.
• There is no user-selects-the-load shortcut here, the way there is for a manual optional standby system. On an emergency system the loads are fixed by the life-safety design, not picked at the switch.
• Selective coordination of the emergency overcurrent devices is a separate requirement, covered at 700.32.
sections.on_the_job: Take a two-story professional building in Winter Garden where the AHJ classes the egress system as emergency. The emergency loads are egress lighting at 6.4 kVA, exit signs at 0.5 kVA and the fire alarm system at 0.9 kVA — 7.8 kVA that all runs together, with nothing the user can shed. Run the Article 220 calculation before anyone promises a generator size, and check the fault-current rating on the transfer gear against the service: the marked rating has to cover the fault current available where the gear connects. If the quoted generator cannot carry the 7.8 kVA, that conversation happens at the quote, not at the first outage.

nec2023_change.change: Emergency capacity now has to cover transients and rapid load swings, and new rules spell out when an emergency source can run in parallel with the normal source or other emergency sources. Size the emergency system for all loads that run together, including rapid load swings and transients like motor starting (700.4(A)).

sections.why_it_exists: When the normal source fails, the emergency system is the only thing between the occupants and a dark stairwell. Gear that fails under fault current, or a source that sags because the load outgrew the calculation, turns a power outage into an evacuation problem. The capacity and rating rules make the system prove on paper, before the emergency, that it can carry every life-safety load at once and survive the worst fault at its terminals.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing the emergency source the way a manual optional standby system is sized — letting the user pick which loads run and adding up only those. Article 700 has no load-picking option: capacity covers every emergency load that operates together. The second trap is checking only capacity and forgetting the rating half of the section; the equipment also has to be suitable for the available fault current.

sections.title: Transfer equipment — emergency systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Emergency transfer equipment has to be automatic, listed and marked for emergency use, and approved by the AHJ. It is built and installed so the emergency source and the other sources cannot be connected together by accident. An automatic transfer switch has to be electrically operated and mechanically held, reconditioned transfer switches are not allowed, the gear may feed only emergency loads, and meter-mounted transfer switches are not permitted for emergency use. The documentation rule of 700.5(E) carries no dwelling exception — unlike 702.5(C) — so the transfer equipment short-circuit rating is field marked on the outside of the gear in dwellings too.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 700.5: When a single feeder carries the emergency loads, redundant transfer equipment or a bypass-isolation transfer switch is now required, so maintenance on the transfer gear doesn't kill emergency power. One feeder supplying the emergency loads now means redundant transfer equipment or a bypass-isolation transfer switch is required (700.5(D)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Read the listing and the marking, not the sales sheet. If the switch is not marked for emergency use, it does not go on a 700 job, however big it is.

sections.title: Signs — emergency sources
sections.plain_explanation:
A sign at the service equipment tells responders and electricians what kind of on-site emergency source the building has and where it is. Nobody should have to hunt through a building during an outage to learn that a second source exists.

The sign sits at the service equipment and states two things: the type of on-site emergency source and where that source is located. It has to be permanent and legible, and it is a different sign from the panel directory — the directory says which loads are emergency; this sign says a second source exists and where to find it. Where the source has its own disconnecting means away from the service, the sign at the service is what lets a responder find and kill both sources.
sections.on_the_job:
Put the source type and location on the sign and check it against the actual disconnect location before you call the job done.

Worked habit: letter the sign before final inspection, then stand at the service and check that a stranger could walk straight to the source from the words on it. A sign that says 'generator' but not where the generator is has not finished this section's job.

sections.title: Surge protection — emergency systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Every emergency system switchboard and panelboard has to have a listed surge protective device. This is a flat requirement of the article, not an upsell and not something to value-engineer out.

The device has to be listed, and it is installed in or on the switchboard or panelboard it protects, connected the way its listing and the manufacturer's instructions direct — short, straight leads matter, because a surge device works through its connection, and a long coiled lead-in adds impedance exactly where the surge arrives. A failed or end-of-life SPD that nobody notices leaves the panel unprotected while looking complete, which is why the device's status indication belongs on the 700.3 test-and-maintenance rounds.
sections.on_the_job: Count an SPD for every emergency panelboard and switchboard on the material list, and confirm it is listed.

sections.title: Wiring — emergency systems stay identified and apart
sections.plain_explanation: Emergency wiring is identified as emergency all the way through: boxes, enclosures, transfer switches, generators and panels are permanently marked, and emergency raceways and cables are marked as emergency at short, regular intervals. Emergency conductors also stay out of enclosures, raceways and cables that carry nonemergency wiring, with only narrow exceptions such as inside transfer equipment. Emergency receptacles are identified by a distinctive color or marking. The identification interval is concrete, not a judgment call: 700.10(A)(2) requires emergency wiring to be marked as emergency at intervals not exceeding 25 ft. And 700.10(D) adds fire protection for emergency feeders in the larger installations it covers — the feeder is protected by a listed electrical circuit protective system, mineral-insulated cable, concrete encasement, or an approved sprinkler-protected space, as the subsection conditions state.
sections.on_the_job: Mark it as you install it, not at trim-out from memory. If a normal circuit and an emergency circuit want the same raceway, stop — that is the exact mix this section exists to prevent.

sections.title: Sources of power — available in 10 seconds
sections.plain_explanation:
When the normal supply fails, emergency power has to be available within 10 seconds. The article lists the permitted kinds of sources, from storage batteries and generator sets to a separate service and unit equipment, and it sets conditions for each one. Engine-driven sources carry on-site fuel rules, battery sources carry a minimum run-time duty at close to full voltage, and the equipment has to be located and designed so one fire, flood or act of vandalism is less likely to kill both supplies at once.

Two numbers carry most of the field weight. A storage battery used as the emergency source has to carry the emergency load for at least 1-1/2 hours without its voltage dropping below 87-1/2 percent of nominal — a battery that fades at 40 minutes is not a 700 source, whatever its amp-hour label says. And the on-site fuel rule for engine-driven sets is part of the source itself: the fuel plan has to be there when the generator is, sized for the run the design requires, not improvised after the outage starts. an internal-combustion prime mover requires an on-premises fuel supply sufficient for not less than 2 hours of full-demand operation.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 700.12: The emergency-source microgrid rule now covers any microgrid, not just dc microgrids, and spells out how designated emergency sources must stay protected when other sources fail. Sources set aside for emergency use can now join a microgrid of any type, ac or dc (700.12(G)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job:
The 10-second clock is the design test. Ask how the source starts, how fast load lands on it, and where its fuel or charge comes from before you argue about brands.

Worked check on the battery duty: a battery string nameplated at 24 V nominal must still be holding at least 21 V (87.5 percent of 24) at the end of a 90-minute full-load run. If the acceptance test did not run the clock and read the voltage, the duty is unproven.

sections.title: Loads on emergency branch circuits
sections.plain_explanation:
Emergency branch circuits feed emergency loads only. A circuit that exists to keep egress lighting and exit signs alive does not pick up convenience loads because there was spare capacity on paper.
• Emergency loads are the life-safety loads classed as emergency by the governmental agency having jurisdiction: egress lighting, exit signs, fire alarm and similar loads.
• General receptacles, office and task lighting, comfort equipment and break-room appliances are not emergency loads, even when the generator is big enough to carry them.
• The limit is about what the load is, not about how much room is left on the circuit or in the panel.
Emergency wiring is identified as emergency as it runs through the building (700.10(A)), so a load that does not belong shows up on the panel schedule before it shows up in the field.
sections.on_the_job: Small medical office in Ocala: a Siemens emergency panel beside the normal panel, with six 20 A branch circuits carrying exit signs, egress lighting over the corridor and stairs, and the fire alarm. During the fit-out, a receptacle for the break-room coffee maker got landed on a spare emergency breaker because it was close. Walk the emergency panel schedule load by load. Anything that is not an emergency load comes off, even if the generator is big enough. The coffee-maker circuit moved to the normal panel before final.

sections.why_it_exists: The emergency source is sized, fueled and tested for one known list of life-safety loads. Every convenience load added to an emergency circuit steals capacity and run time from that list. The theft shows up at the worst moment: during a real outage, with the building occupied, the source overloads or runs short while people are still on the stairs.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is: the generator has capacity to spare, so one more receptacle circuit on the emergency panel is fine. 700.15 does not ration emergency circuits by capacity. It rations them by load type. If the load is not an emergency load, it does not go on an emergency branch circuit, however big the source is.

Emergency panel schedule lists loads that were never installed, and installed loads that are not listed.
Spare emergency breaker used for a later tenant load without re-checking the emergency load list.

sections.title: Emergency illumination — no single failure leaves a space dark
sections.plain_explanation: Emergency illumination covers the means of egress lighting, the illuminated exit signs and every other luminaire specified as necessary to get people out. The system has to be designed and installed so that the failure of any single illumination source cannot leave a space that requires emergency illumination in total darkness — one dead lamp, ballast or driver never blacks out an exit path. Control devices on the system have to be listed for use in emergency systems. Where discharge lighting such as HID is the sole source of normal illumination, the emergency system has to operate until normal illumination is restored, because those lamps are slow to restrike. The section also requires emergency illumination in the area of an indoor service or feeder disconnecting means.
sections.on_the_job: Count sources, not fixtures on a schedule. Stand in each egress space and ask what goes dark if one source dies; if the answer is everything, the layout fails this section even though every fixture sits on an emergency circuit.

sections.title: Branch-circuit emergency lighting transfer switch (700.25)
sections.plain_explanation: 700.25 covers the branch-circuit emergency lighting transfer switch: where emergency lighting is served from a branch circuit, a listed transfer switch at the branch-circuit level is the device that moves that lighting load to the emergency source when normal power fails, so the egress lighting does not depend on an upstream decision. It is a narrow, listed-device rule — the switch, its listing and its wiring follow the printed section and the design documents. Edition note: this page states the NEC 2020 rule Florida enforces; any 2023 change is confirmed against the printed 2023 text before it is taught here.
sections.on_the_job: Emergency-system design is engineered work. If a plan shows branch-circuit transfer switches for egress lighting, land them exactly as the drawings and the device listing say, and flag any field change to the designer — do not re-feed egress lighting on your own call.

sections.title: Selective coordination — emergency systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Every overcurrent device in an emergency system has to selectively coordinate with all supply-side overcurrent protective devices. Selective coordination means that for any fault the system can deliver, only the device closest to the fault opens: the branch device clears a branch fault while the feeder and service devices stay closed.
• The coordination has to hold across the full range of overcurrents available at each point, not just at one fault level.
• A licensed professional engineer or another qualified person selects the devices and performs the coordination design.
• The coordination documentation has to be available to the people who design, install, inspect, maintain, and operate the system.
That is why a breaker swap or a settings change on an emergency system is an engineering event, not a parts swap.
sections.on_the_job: On a small medical office in Winter Park with a generator feeding a Siemens emergency distribution panel, the coordination study called out specific breaker frames and trip settings at the main, the feeder, and each branch. When the specified branch breaker was back-ordered, the crew did not substitute a same-ampere breaker from stock: a different trip curve can erase the coordination the study proved. The substitute waited for the engineer's written approval, and the study, device list, and settings went into the job record, where the owner and the AHJ can ask for them.

nec2023_change.change: Selective coordination on emergency systems now has to be rechecked after any overcurrent device replacement and after any change to the system. New 700.32(B): replace an emergency overcurrent device and coordination has to be reevaluated.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 700.32 Emergency selective coordination

sections.why_it_exists: An emergency system exists for the worst ten minutes of a building's life: a fire, a blackout, people feeling their way down the stairs. If a fault on one egress-lighting branch trips the emergency main instead of its own branch device, the whole building goes dark at the exact moment the system was installed to prevent. Selective coordination keeps a local fault local, so exit signs, fire alarm, and the rest of the egress lighting stay alive while the faulted branch is isolated.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that devices coordinate because their ampere ratings step down in size — a big main feeding a smaller feeder feeding a small branch breaker. Rating steps alone prove nothing. 700.32 requires the devices to be selected so that only the device protecting the faulted circuit opens, across the full range of overcurrents, and a qualified person has to design it and document it.

sections.title: Legally required standby systems — the middle tier
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 701 covers standby power that a law, code or AHJ requires, but that is not classed as emergency. These systems back up loads that aid firefighting and rescue, control health hazards, or keep ventilation, smoke removal, sewage, communications and similar loads running so an emergency does not get worse. They sit below Article 700 in priority: a 700 load always outranks a 701 load on a shared source. If nobody with authority required the system, it is not 701 — it is optional standby under 702.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:

• 701.4(D): Added language that now identifies the two different types of parallel operation, normal and alternate sources, of legally required systems in new Section 701.4(D).

sections.title: Transfer equipment — legally required standby
sections.plain_explanation: Transfer equipment for a legally required standby system has to be automatic, listed and marked for that use, and approved by the AHJ, and it has to keep the standby source from being interconnected with the other sources by accident. Automatic transfer switches are electrically operated and mechanically held, reconditioned switches are not allowed, and meter-mounted transfer switches are not permitted here either. The transfer equipment short-circuit rating is field marked on the outside of the gear.
sections.on_the_job: Same discipline as 700: check the marking for legally required standby use before the gear is ordered, not after it is hung.

sections.title: Wiring — legally required standby may share raceways
sections.plain_explanation:
Unlike emergency wiring, legally required standby wiring is allowed to run in the same raceways, boxes and cabinets as general wiring. The strict separation duty belongs to Article 700: emergency conductors stay out of raceways, boxes and cables that carry nonemergency wiring, with only narrow exceptions, such as inside transfer equipment (700.10). Article 701 carries no such rule.
• Importing the 700 separation duty into a 701 job wastes raceways, boxes and labor the Code never asked for.
• Forgetting the separation on a 700 job is a violation.
• The wiring method follows the classification, so settle which article the system is under before the first raceway goes in.
sections.on_the_job: Community clubhouse in Marion County, with a sewage lift station and smoke-control fans on a legally required standby system. The standby feeder and the general feeders share the same raceway run out to the pump house. That is legal under 701.10, and it saved a second run. The same building's emergency lighting is Article 700 work, and those conductors stayed in their own raceway, start to finish. Know which article the job is under before you decide how to run the raceways. The wiring method follows the classification, not habit.

Legally required standby loads — smoke control, sewage, ventilation — keep an emergency from getting worse, and the Code accepts the shared-raceway risk for them. The law already weighed it; that is why sharing is legal here.

sections.title: Sources of power — available in 60 seconds
sections.plain_explanation:
Legally required standby power has to be available within 60 seconds of the normal supply failing — slower than the 10 seconds of Article 700, far faster than a portable generator someone drags out of a garage. The article lists the permitted source types and their conditions, including on-site fuel for engine-driven sources and battery duty where batteries are the source. One source may also carry optional loads only where capacity is truly there, or where automatic pickup and shedding protect the legally required loads first.

The battery duty mirrors the emergency tier: a storage battery source has to supply and maintain the legally required load for at least 1-1/2 hours without the voltage falling below 87-1/2 percent of nominal. Note that this chapter asks two different questions of a battery system — the 60-second availability clock above, and the 90-minute endurance duty here — and a system can pass one and fail the other.

sections.title: Selective coordination — legally required standby
sections.plain_explanation: Legally required standby overcurrent devices have to selectively coordinate with all supply-side overcurrent protective devices, so a fault on one standby branch opens the device at the fault instead of tripping devices upstream and darkening healthy standby loads with it. The coordination is selected by a licensed professional engineer or another qualified person engaged primarily in the design, installation or maintenance of electrical systems, and the selection has to be documented and made available to the people authorized to design, install, inspect, maintain and operate the system. It is the Article 700 duty at 700.32 carried one tier down. Coordination is not required between two devices in series where no loads are connected in parallel with the downstream device.
sections.on_the_job: Same discipline as the emergency tier: this is a study, not a field adjustment. Get the documented coordination selection into the job record before the gear is released, and leave it where the inspector and the owner's maintenance people can reach it.

sections.title: Optional standby systems — home and business generators
sections.plain_explanation: Article 702 covers standby systems nobody required: the homeowner who wants the fridge, well pump and a few lights through a Florida outage, or the business protecting product and comfort. Life safety does not depend on these systems, and that single fact is what keeps them out of Articles 700 and 701. The article still regulates them hard where it counts: capacity, transfer equipment that can never tie the generator to the utility by accident, signs, wiring and outdoor generator sets. Portable generators that are never connected to the premises wiring are outside this article; the moment one is connected through an inlet and transfer equipment, 702 is in play.
sections.on_the_job: Most Sharma generator work lives here. Start every quote by sorting the loads into what runs automatically, what the owner will switch by hand, and what never runs on the generator.
sections.sharma_note: S-02: transfer equipment Sharma furnishes is Siemens. S-09 only enters if the standby work changes the meter/panel layout.

sections.florida_note: Florida hurricane season is why this article earns its keep here — but no Florida amendment relaxes the transfer or sizing rules in this chapter. The AHJ and the printed NEC 2020 govern.

sections.title: Available fault current — optional standby equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Optional standby equipment has to be suitable for the maximum available short-circuit current at its terminals. That is a different rating from the amp rating. A transfer switch can match the load exactly — 200 A switch on a 200 A service — and still be the wrong switch, because its short-circuit current rating sits below what the service can deliver into a fault.
• Get the available fault current before ordering: from the utility, or from the field marking on the service equipment. Other than in dwelling units, service equipment is marked with the maximum available fault current and the date it was figured (110.24).
• Compare that number with the short-circuit current rating marked on the transfer equipment, not with its amp rating.
• The same duty runs through the rest of the circuit: interrupting ratings (110.9) and the short-circuit current ratings of the components (110.10) must suit the fault current at their terminals.
sections.on_the_job: Strip-center tenant in Marion County: 200 A service, standby generator for the coolers and lights. The marking on the service gear read 22,000 A available fault current. The first transfer switch in the quote was a 200 A switch with a 10,000 A short-circuit rating: right amps, wrong fault duty, and it went back. The switch that stayed is rated 22,000 A. Pull the available fault current from the service gear or the utility information and match the transfer equipment rating to it before ordering, not at rough-in.

sections.why_it_exists: A bolted fault at the switch does not draw load current. It draws everything the utility transformer can push until an overcurrent device clears, and the switch has to survive those cycles without welding its contacts shut or coming apart. A switch that fails closed can also tie the generator to the utility, the one connection transfer equipment exists to prevent.

sections.title: System capacity — the sizing fork in Article 702
sections.plain_explanation: How big the standby source must be depends on how the load gets onto it. With manual transfer, the user chooses the load, so the source only has to carry what is intended to run at one time. With automatic transfer, nobody is standing there choosing, so the source is sized to the calculated load — figured under Article 220 or by another approved method — and it must either carry the full transferred load or be paired with automatic load management. This page and the two that follow were re-checked against 2020 sources for this edition, because the v1 wording on this section was flagged unverified.
sections.on_the_job: Write down which side of the fork the job is on before you size anything. 'Automatic transfer, partial load, no load management' is not a third option.
sections.figure_idea: Original diagram: a fork in a road — left branch MANUAL with a hand picking load switches, right branch AUTOMATIC splitting again into FULL LOAD and LOAD MANAGEMENT.

sections.title: Manual transfer — the user selects the load
sections.plain_explanation: Where manual transfer equipment is used, the optional standby system has to be able to supply all the equipment intended to be operated at one time, and the user is permitted to select which loads are connected. That selection is what sets the practical size of the source: a homeowner who will run the fridge, a few lights and the well pump — and leave the range and dryer off — does not need a generator sized for the whole house.
sections.on_the_job: Build the intended-load list with the owner and put it in the job record. If a load is not on the list, it does not get counted, and it does not get promised.

sections.title: Automatic transfer — full load, or load management
sections.plain_explanation: Where automatic transfer equipment is used, the standby source is sized to the calculated load, figured under Article 220 or by another approved method — for an existing installation, recorded maximum demand is one of the approved routes the code recognizes through 220.87. The system then has to satisfy one of two duties. Under the full-load duty, the source carries the entire load the automatic equipment transfers. Under the load-management duty, an automatic system manages the connected load and the source only has to carry the maximum load that management system will actually connect.
sections.on_the_job: Do the Article 220 calculation or pull the demand data first, then check which duty the design claims. A load-management claim needs the actual listed management equipment on the job, not a promise that the owner will turn things off.

sections.title: Transfer equipment — required, listed, and built to keep sources apart
sections.plain_explanation: Transfer equipment is required to connect an optional standby source to the premises wiring, and in the 2020 code it has to be listed — a tightening over earlier editions that catches unlisted interlock hardware. One narrow exception exists: a temporary portable generator connection without transfer equipment, only where maintenance and supervision ensure qualified persons service it and the normal supply is physically isolated by a lockable disconnect or by disconnecting the normal conductors. The four duties that follow it in the section — meter-mounted switches, documentation, inadvertent interconnection, and parallel operation — get their own pages next, in the section's own order.
sections.on_the_job: Default answer on a house: a listed transfer switch or a listed interlock arrangement, installed so utility and generator can never meet. If a product cannot show its listing, it does not go in, whatever its paperwork claims about being tested on someone else's panel.
sections.sharma_note: S-02: transfer equipment Sharma furnishes is Siemens, and it still has to carry the listing this section requires.

sections.title: Meter-mounted transfer switches
sections.plain_explanation:
A transfer switch that mounts in the meter socket — between the utility meter and its enclosure — is allowed for optional standby systems, but only as a listed meter-mounted transfer switch.
• Manual operation is the default: a meter-mounted switch is manual unless it is rated in accordance with the automatic-transfer sizing duty of 702.4(B)(2).
• The meter socket is not a loophole around generator sizing: automatic transfer still has to meet the same capacity rules as any other automatic switch, sized to the calculated load or paired with automatic load management.
• The contrast to remember: Articles 700 and 701 do not permit meter-mounted transfer switches at all. This device exists only in the optional standby world of Article 702.
sections.on_the_job: For a standby generator at a single-family home in Oviedo, the listed meter-mounted transfer switch kept the job simple: no separate transfer switch on the wall, and manual transfer — the homeowner starts the generator and transfers by hand. Because the switch was manual, the automatic sizing duty of 702.4(B)(2) never came into play. The utility still had to approve the work in its meter socket before the seal was cut, and that approval was separate from the county electrical inspection.
sections.why_it_exists: The meter socket is the one point where utility equipment, the service, and the premises wiring all meet, and it was never designed as a switch enclosure. A listed meter-mounted transfer switch is built and tested for that spot: interrupting service current and keeping the generator from ever backfeeding the utility. An unlisted gadget in the socket risks the life of a lineman working a line he was told was dead.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'permitted anywhere a transfer switch is permitted.' Meter-mounted transfer switches are an Article 702-only device: Articles 700 and 701 forbid them outright. The second trap is calling every meter-mounted switch automatic. It is manual unless it carries the rating 702.4(B)(2) demands for automatic operation.

sections.title: Documentation — short-circuit rating marked on the gear
sections.plain_explanation:
On jobs other than dwelling units, the short-circuit current rating of the transfer equipment has to be field marked on the outside of the equipment. Not inside the door, and not left in the submittal package: on the outside, where the next person to work on the gear sees it.
• The marking states the rating the equipment was installed for, so it is read off the equipment data after the 702.4(A) fault-current match is made.
• The person maintaining or replacing that gear years later should not need the original submittal to learn what fault duty it was built for.
• Dwelling units are the exception in this paragraph. The marking duty here is for other-than-dwelling work.
sections.on_the_job: Same strip-center tenant as the fault-current check: once the switch rated 22,000 A was in, the rating went on the outside of the enclosure — short-circuit current rating: 22,000 A — as a durable field marking, and a photo of the finished marking went into the job record. Carry a marker and the rating from the equipment data to every non-dwelling transfer install, and photograph the finished marking for the job record.

Two identical-looking switches can carry different short-circuit ratings, and a service upgrade can raise the available fault current years after the switch went in. The outside marking is the one place the installed rating survives lost paperwork, staff changes and repainted enclosures, and it is what an inspector checks against the service marking. It also settles the question at final inspection in seconds: the rating is on the gear, in the open, or the job is not finished.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that the factory nameplate already lists a rating, so nothing has to be added in the field. On other-than-dwelling 702 jobs, 702.5(C) wants the short-circuit current rating field marked on the outside of the equipment, whatever the nameplate inside the door says.

sections.title: Inadvertent interconnection — the heart of 702.5
sections.plain_explanation: Transfer equipment has to be suitable for the job, listed, and designed and installed so that all sources of supply can never be inadvertently interconnected in any operation of the equipment. This is the rule that kills backfeeding: a generator pushing power out through the service can energize a line a utility crew believes is dead. The listing requirement in this paragraph is the 2020 change that unlisted interlock hardware runs into.
sections.on_the_job: Test the finished install through every switch position, not just the normal one. The duty covers any operation of the equipment, including the sloppy one nobody planned.

sections.title: Parallel installation — Article 705 takes over
sections.plain_explanation:
Transfer equipment and electric power production systems installed to operate in parallel with the normal source also have to comply with Article 705.
• A standby source that only ever replaces the utility is a 702 job: transfer equipment, and no interconnection.
• The moment a source is meant to operate alongside the utility, the interconnection rules of Article 705 join the transfer rules.
• On a parallel job the two articles are not either/or: 702 governs the transfer, 705 governs the handshake with the live source.
sections.on_the_job: Ask one question on every generator quote: will this source ever run in parallel with the utility? A homeowner in Lake Mary wants a standby set that only takes over in an outage — that is a 702 job, priced and wired as transfer equipment. A small commercial customer who wants the generator to parallel the utility for peak shaving gets a different answer: the same transfer gear, plus an Article 705 interconnection — connection point, busbar and conductor checks, and marking that tells the next electrician a second source exists. Price and wire it as both, or do not sell it as parallel.

sections.why_it_exists: A source connected to a live utility system can backfeed conductors, fight the utility's protection, and keep a 'dead' service energized. Article 705 exists for exactly that handshake — where the source may connect, how much current the connection and the busbar may carry, and how the equipment is marked so the next person knows a second source exists. A parallel source wired to transfer rules alone skips every one of those protections.

The reverse trap also fails — a standby source that never operates in parallel does not pick up Article 705 just because a generator is present.

sections.title: Signs — standby sources, and the power inlet sign
sections.plain_explanation:
Signs close the loop that transfer equipment starts. At service equipment, a sign identifies the type and location of each on-site optional standby source — for a house, the sign sits at the 230.85 emergency disconnect and points to the permanently installed standby source disconnect or the means to shut down the prime mover. Where a power inlet is used for a portable generator, a sign at the inlet states which kind of generator system may be connected there: a separately derived (bonded neutral) system only, or a nonseparately derived (floating neutral) system only.

sections.title: Wiring — optional standby wiring may share raceways
sections.plain_explanation:
Optional standby wiring is allowed to occupy the same raceways, cables, boxes and cabinets as other wiring. That permission is the opposite of the Article 700 rule, where emergency conductors stay independent of nonemergency wiring.
• The permission covers the whole run: raceways, cables, boxes and cabinets.
• It is one more reason the classification question comes first: the same physical run can be legal under 702 and a violation under 700.
• The permission is not a shortcut around the identification, transfer equipment and sign rules elsewhere in this article. It answers only the raceway question.
• Sharing the raceway does not merge the systems. The standby circuits still have to be findable later, which is why they stay identified in the panel directory.
sections.on_the_job: New slab home in Ocala with a permanently installed standby generator on a 200 A Siemens service. The generator feeder shares the underground run and the panel gutter with the normal circuits. That is permitted under 702.10, and it kept the job to one trench. Use the permission, but keep the standby circuits identified in the panel directory so the next electrician knows what the generator feeds: refrigerator, well pump and kitchen lights, marked as standby circuits in the directory.

Nobody's escape route depends on it, so the Code does not buy it the expensive protection of separate raceways. sections.title: Outdoor portable generators
sections.plain_explanation: 702.11 covers the portable generator that lives in the garage and rolls out to the driveway when the power fails. The disconnect relief is exact: under 702.11(B), a portable generator rated 15 kW or less, connected through a flanged inlet or other cord-and-plug connection, does not need an additional disconnecting means where its ungrounded conductors serve or pass through a building. Under 702.11(A), permanently installed generators and portable generators over 15 kW need a readily accessible disconnect per 445.18, within sight of the building, for that relief. The connection to the house is still through listed transfer equipment and a proper power inlet (702.12(C) covers inlets 100 A and up); a cord through a window to a dryer receptacle is backfeeding, not a connection method. The neutral question decides the transfer equipment: whether the portable set's neutral is bonded to its frame determines whether the transfer switch must switch the neutral, and the generator's documentation — not habit — answers it.
sections.on_the_job: Hurricane setup: inlet box on the outside wall, listed transfer equipment or an interlocked breaker inside, generator outdoors and clear of windows and doors while it runs. Check the set's neutral bonding before you choose the transfer switch, and label the inlet for the size of set it accepts.
sections.figure_idea: House elevation: outdoor inlet, generator placement clear of openings, cord run.

sections.title: Outdoor generator sets — when a building disconnect is not required
sections.plain_explanation: For permanently installed generators and portable generators over 15 kW used outdoors, if the generator has a readily accessible disconnect within sight of the building it supplies, no extra disconnect is required at the building — provided that generator disconnect is in accordance with 445.18, and where the generator supply conductors terminate at a disconnecting means in or on the building, that disconnect meets 225.36. For a portable generator of 15 kW or less connected through a flanged inlet or another cord-and-plug connection, no disconnecting means is required at the building for the ungrounded conductors serving or passing through it. Both rules are about not duplicating a disconnect that already does the job — neither one removes the transfer-equipment duty in 702.5.
sections.on_the_job: Confirm the generator's own disconnect is readily accessible and within sight before you rely on the first rule, and confirm the rating and the flanged inlet before you rely on the second.

sections.title: Power inlets 100 A and up — listed, with an interlocked disconnect
sections.plain_explanation: Where a portable generator connects through an inlet rated 100 amps or more, the 2020 code adds two requirements on the inlet equipment. The equipment must be listed for the intended use, and it must be provided with an interlocked disconnecting means, so the inlet arrangement cannot leave the building connected the wrong way. Two exceptions soften it: the inlet device itself may serve as the disconnecting means where it is rated for that duty, and supervised industrial installations with a permanent generator space within line of sight follow their own conditions. Below 100 amps this paragraph does not apply — the 702.12(A) and (B) rules on the previous page govern instead.
sections.on_the_job: On a big portable hookup, read the inlet's listing and find the interlock before you land conductors. If the inlet is 100 A or more and there is no interlocked disconnect, that is a stop-and-call, not a field fix.

sections.title: Interconnected electric power production sources
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 705 governs sources that operate in parallel with another source — most often a solar inverter, storage system or generator tied to a live utility service. It answers three practical questions: where may the source connect, how much current may the connection and the busbar carry, and how does everyone after you know the extra source exists. Connections land on the supply side under 705.11 or the load side under 705.12, and a power control system under 705.13 can change the math. Article 690 in Chapter 6 governs the solar array itself; this article governs its handshake with the premises wiring.

sections.on_the_job: Decide supply side or load side on paper first. The choice drives the overcurrent protection, the busbar math and the labels, in that order.

sections.title: Identification of power sources — the directory
sections.plain_explanation: Where sources are interconnected, a permanent plaque or directory at the service equipment — or another approved, readily visible location — shows where every parallel power source disconnect is. The plaque carries the caution that multiple sources of power are present, and any diagram on it has to be oriented the way the building actually sits. This is the page a firefighter or a utility worker reads; it has to be right, not approximate.
sections.on_the_job: Walk the building and verify every disconnect location before the plaque is made. A directory that points to where the disconnect was planned, instead of where it is, fails its only job.

sections.title: Supply-side source connections
sections.plain_explanation:
A source may connect on the supply side of the service disconnect, at the points the service rules allow, under its own set of conditions for conductor sizing, overcurrent protection and grounding. A supply-side connection steps around the panelboard busbar limits entirely, which is why it is the escape route when the 120 percent math in 705.12 will not close. It trades that freedom for service-level work: the connection is ahead of the main, so its protection and its disconnecting means have to be planned like service equipment.

• 705.11: Conductors from a supply-side tie-in to a power source's disconnect are now service conductors, so the Article 230 and 250 service rules govern them. The 2020 inside-building length limits dropped out. Conductors from the tie-in to the power source's disconnect are service conductors now, and that disconnect is a service disconnect located like one (230.70(A)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Price a supply-side tap as service work, with utility coordination, not as 'one more breaker.' If the busbar math fails, compare this route honestly against derating the main.

sections.title: Load-side source connections — the shape of the rule
sections.plain_explanation: A source output may connect on the load side of the other source's service disconnect, at any distribution equipment on the premises. Where that equipment is fed by two sources at once and feeds branch circuits or feeders, the connection has to satisfy the sub-rules that follow: a dedicated breaker or fusible disconnect for each source, the busbar and conductor ampere-rating methods, marking of equipment that contains more than one source, breakers suitable for backfeed, and fastening where a backfed breaker could work loose. Where a power control system is installed under 705.13, the controller setting stands in for the source output current in these calculations.
sections.on_the_job: Work the sub-rules in order on the plan, not at the panel with the cover off. By trim-out, the breaker position and size are already decided by this section.
sections.figure_idea: Original diagram: a panel bus drawn vertically, main at the top, loads in the middle, source breaker at the bottom, with callouts for dedicated breaker, marking and hold-down.

sections.title: Dedicated overcurrent and disconnect — each source gets its own
sections.plain_explanation:
Each source interconnection is made at its own dedicated circuit breaker or fusible disconnecting means. Two inverters do not share one breaker because the math happened to fit, and a source does not land on a breaker that also feeds a load.
• One source system, one dedicated device — every time.
• The dedicated device is both the overcurrent protection point for the interconnection and the place that source is disconnected.
• A breaker that feeds loads is never an interconnection point, and a source breaker never doubles as a load breaker.
sections.on_the_job: A small commercial rooftop in Clermont gets two string inverters: one with a 32 A maximum output current, one with 16 A. On the takeoff that is two dedicated breakers in the panel — a 40 A for the first inverter and a 20 A for the second, each sized from its own inverter's continuous output, and neither breaker feeds anything else. When a panel schedule shows one 60 A breaker with both inverters landed on it because the total 'fit,' send it back: 705.12(A) counts sources, not sums.

sections.why_it_exists: A shared breaker hides what is feeding the bus. Open the wrong device and a source is still backfeeding the panel while someone works in it; trip one shared device and two sources drop together, or a source ends up protected at a rating that has nothing to do with its own output. A dedicated device per source makes each source visible, protected at its own rating, and disconnectable on its own.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer lands two inverters on one breaker sized for their combined output, because the total ampacity works. 705.12(A) is not an ampacity rule — it is a one-device-per-source rule. The second trap lands a source on a breaker that also feeds a load; a dedicated device serves its source and nothing else.

sections.title: The 100 percent busbar method — breaker anywhere
sections.plain_explanation: The plainest load-side method: 125 percent of the source output current, plus the rating of the overcurrent device protecting the busbar, must not exceed the busbar ampacity itself. Meet that sum and the source breaker may sit anywhere on the bus. Fail it and you do not argue with the arithmetic — you move to one of the other methods in 705.12(B)(3), derate something, or go to the supply side.
sections.on_the_job: Run this method first because it is the one with no position condition. Example in the lookup entries: on a 225A bus with a 200A main, this method leaves room for only a 20A inverter output, while the 120 percent method on the next page leaves much more.

sections.title: The 120 percent rule — sources at opposite ends
sections.plain_explanation: Where two sources sit at opposite ends of a busbar that carries loads, the same sum — 125 percent of the source output current plus the rating of the device protecting the busbar — may go up to 120 percent of the busbar ampacity. The busbar still has to be sized for the connected loads under Article 220. Because the allowance depends on position, a permanent warning label goes on the distribution equipment next to the backfed breaker, warning that it is a power source output connection and must not be relocated. On the common 200A bus with a 200A main, this method allows 40A of backfeed device capacity, which is a 32A inverter output — the worked example already in v1 as L-092 and Q-063.
sections.on_the_job: Three field checks, every time: sources truly at opposite ends, the math done with 125 percent of output (not the breaker size), and the do-not-relocate label on before inspection. Moving that breaker 'a couple of spaces' on a later service call quietly breaks the method.
sections.sharma_note: S-03 matters here on existing work: in an existing Square D panel, the backfed breaker is a Square D breaker listed for that panel — the 120 percent math never licenses a mixed-brand breaker.
sections.figure_idea: Original diagram: a horizontal busbar, utility breaker at the left end, solar breaker at the right end, loads tapped between them, and the warning label drawn beside the solar breaker.

sections.title: The sum-of-breakers method
sections.plain_explanation: A third load-side method ignores the main breaker rating and adds up the ampere ratings of all the overcurrent devices on the panelboard — load and supply devices together, excluding the device protecting the busbar — and that total must not exceed the busbar ampacity. Equipment using this method carries permanent warning labels at the distribution equipment identifying that all sources are present. It fits panels where the breaker population, not the main, is the honest limit.
sections.on_the_job: Count every breaker that is actually in the panel, including the source breaker, and write the sum in the job record. A panel that passes today can fail this method after one added circuit.

sections.title: The center-fed busbar method — one end only
sections.plain_explanation: Some dwelling panelboards are center-fed: the main breaker or main lugs sit in the middle of the busbar instead of at one end, a construction common on combination meter-and-panel equipment in some regions. This method permits a source connection at either end of that busbar, but never at both ends. The math is the familiar 120 percent check applied to the connection: the sum of 125 percent of the power source output circuit current and the rating of the overcurrent device protecting the busbar must not exceed 120 percent of the busbar rating. Because a center-fed bus can concentrate load on one half of the busbar, the option is limited to dwellings.
sections.on_the_job: Identify the panel construction before reaching for the 120 percent rule: if the main sits in the middle, this paragraph is the method, not (3)(2). Land the source at one end only, run the math on that connection, and record which end was used in the job file.

sections.title: Power control systems — a listed controller can limit the current
sections.plain_explanation:
New in the 2020 code, this section recognizes a power control system: listed equipment that monitors and limits how much current a source puts onto conductors and busbars. Where one is installed, its controller setting is treated as the source output current for the 705.11 and 705.12 calculations, so a system set to a lower limit can fit a panel the raw inverter rating could not. The section also guards the settings themselves, because the whole method stands on the setting staying where it was set.

sections.title: Disconnecting means for sources
sections.plain_explanation:
Every interconnected source needs a disconnecting means that meets this section, which in 2020 gathered the source disconnect rules into one place. The disconnect has to separate the source from the conductors of the other systems, and where a disconnect that unqualified people can reach would expose live parts when open, it has to be locked or need a tool to open. A source that can energize a panel from the far end is exactly the surprise this section exists to remove.

sections.title: Overcurrent protection — interconnected sources
sections.plain_explanation:
Conductors and equipment on an interconnected system get overcurrent protection under 705.30, working with the circuit-current sizing in 705.28 and with Article 240.
• Protection from all sources (705.30(A)). A conductor fed from both ends can be overcurrented from either direction, so protection is planned for the source output the same way it is planned for a utility feed.
• Device ratings follow the calculated source currents. The source output current is the nameplate current (705.28), and conductors and overcurrent devices are sized at not less than 125% of that maximum current — the continuous-output factor is built in.
• Equipment containing overcurrent devices supplied from more than one power source is marked to indicate that all sources are present (705.30(C)).
• A circuit breaker not marked line and load is suitable for backfeed; one marked line and load is not (705.30(D)).
sections.on_the_job: On a small commercial rooftop in Orlando, the interactive inverter's nameplate continuous output is 32 A. Sharma sizes the output conductors and the backfed breaker at 125% — 32 × 1.25 = 40 A — using a Siemens 40 A breaker that is not marked line and load. The panelboard is marked for multiple sources, because that panel is now fed from two directions and the next person who opens it needs to know.

Protection planned only around the utility feed leaves the conductor exposed to the inverter or generator feeding it backwards, and fault current does not care which end it came from. The marking and backfeed rules exist because the second source is invisible until somebody opens the wrong device.

sections.title: Loss of primary source — the source must stop and stay off
sections.plain_explanation: When the primary source — normally the utility — is lost, an interconnected power production source has to be automatically disconnected from all ungrounded conductors of the primary source, and it must not reconnect until the primary source is restored. The duty bites even if only one line or phase of the utility supply opens. It exists so a solar array or cogeneration source can never backfeed lines that utility crews are treating as dead. The exception is the listed utility-interactive inverter: it may keep producing ac power for local loads as long as no power reaches the service conductors, which in effect turns the premises into their own island. A source serving an emergency or legally required standby system through transfer equipment is not shut down by this section — those systems are supposed to run during the outage.
sections.on_the_job: This is why a grid-tied inverter goes quiet in an outage even in full sun: it is not broken, it is obeying this section. If the owner wants power during outages, the answer is equipment designed to island legally, never a defeated anti-islanding control.

sections.title: Energy storage systems — batteries under the code
sections.plain_explanation: Article 706 covers energy storage systems over 1 kWh that can feed a premises wiring system, on their own or alongside other sources. Only qualified persons install and maintain these systems, each system is listed, and its nameplate carries the ratings the installer and the inspector both work from. The two hazards that shape the article are stored energy that is still live when everything looks off, and fault current a battery bank can deliver without any utility behind it. Dwellings get extra attention: the disconnect a first responder can reach, and a dc voltage limit inside the home — 100 volts between conductors or to ground, with up to 600 volts allowed where live parts are not accessible during routine maintenance (706.20(B)).
sections.on_the_job: Treat every ESS terminal as live until you have proved otherwise with a meter. 'The inverter is off' is not a test result.
sections.figure_idea: Original diagram: a battery cabinet, an inverter and a panel, with a bold disconnect symbol between the batteries and everything else, and a 'stored energy stays live' callout on the battery side.
sections.florida_note: Florida note: hurricane-driven battery work is arriving in houses that were never designed for it. The ESS rules in this article, plus the fire-code siting the AHJ enforces, both apply — ask the AHJ about location limits before the batteries are set.

sections.title: Commissioning and maintenance — energy storage
sections.plain_explanation:
Away from one- and two-family dwellings, an energy storage system is commissioned when it is installed. Every system — dwellings included — is kept maintained in proper and safe operating condition, following the manufacturer instructions and industry standards.
• Commissioning proves the installed system works as a system: connections, controls and protective functions checked and documented at installation.
• Maintenance is not optional, and it is not guesswork: the manufacturer's instructions set the tasks.
• Storage is not fit-and-forget equipment: connections, ventilation, controls and firmware all age.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma wires a listed battery system — over 1 kWh, so Article 706 applies — at a small warehouse in Orlando. Because it is not a one- or two-family dwelling, the system is commissioned at installation: operation verified, settings and protective functions checked, and the commissioning record written up. Hand over the commissioning record and the maintenance instructions with the job. If the owner cannot say who maintains the system, that conversation happens at sale, not at the first fault.

sections.why_it_exists: A battery system stores enough energy to hurt someone on a day when every switch looks off. Connections loosen and heat, ventilation gets blocked by stored material, firmware and protective settings drift — and none of it announces itself until the system is asked to perform, or fails hot. Commissioning catches the installation errors on day one; maintenance catches the aging before it becomes a fire or a dead system.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating commissioning as a rule for every installation. In the 2020 text the commissioning duty stops at one- and two-family dwellings — but the maintenance duty does not: a dwelling system still has to be maintained in proper and safe operating condition. The second trap: 'commissioned' does not mean 'turned on once.' It means tested, verified and documented.
inspection_fails: Battery system in a commercial space turned over with no commissioning performed or documented.
No commissioning record or maintenance instructions handed to the owner at turnover.
Storage system found with its ventilation blocked and connections never re-checked — no maintenance since installation.
Protective settings and firmware never verified after installation.

sections.title: Disconnecting means — energy storage systems
sections.plain_explanation:
A disconnecting means has to separate the storage system from the other power sources, the utilization equipment and the premises wiring, and integral disconnects in listed equipment can do that job. The disconnect is readily accessible, at the system or within sight of it, it plainly shows whether it is open or closed, and it is permanently marked as the energy storage system disconnect, with the system's nominal ac voltage, maximum dc voltage and available fault current marked where the section requires them. For a house, the disconnect or its remote control sits at a readily accessible spot outside the building, where responders can reach it. The marking package in 706.15 also calls for an arc-flash warning label, and where the label is based on an arc-flash hazard analysis it carries the date that analysis was performed. Items (2), (3) and (4) of that marking list are waived for energy storage systems in one- and two-family dwellings.

• 706.15: A field-serviceable battery installed apart from its energy storage system (ESS) electronics now gets a dedicated disconnect within sight, string breaks above 240 volts and a hazard label. A field-serviceable battery located away from its ESS electronics now needs a readily accessible disconnect, within sight of the battery, opening every ungrounded conductor (706.15(E)).

sections.on_the_job: Mark it, then stand at the service and ask: could a responder who has never seen this house find and open this disconnect? If not, the install is not finished.

sections.title: Circuit sizing and overcurrent protection — storage circuits
sections.plain_explanation:
Storage circuit currents come from the nameplate ratings (706.30(A)), and the rest of the sizing follows from them:
• For an ESS circuit, use the nameplate-rated current. For an inverter, use its continuous output current on the ac side, and its continuous input current at the lowest input voltage on the dc side.
• Conductors must have an ampacity at least the greater of the nameplate current or the rating of the overcurrent device protecting them (706.30(B)).
• The overcurrent protection that follows in 706.31 must be rated not less than 125% of the 706.30 current, unless the assembly, overcurrent devices included, is listed for operation at 100% of its rating (706.31(B)).
• On the dc side, devices must be listed for dc use, with the appropriate voltage, current and interrupting ratings (706.31(C)). Battery circuits punish borrowed ac-only habits: a device that cannot interrupt dc fault current is not protection, whatever its amp number says.
sections.on_the_job: On a solar-plus-storage house in Winter Garden, the ESS inverter's nameplate continuous output is 40 A, so the ac breaker is 50 A — 40 × 1.25 — and the conductors are sized to that breaker, not to the 40 A nameplate. On the dc side, read the dc rating on every fuse and breaker in the battery circuit out loud during the rough-in inspection of your own work. If it does not say dc, it comes out.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A battery bank is a fault-current machine sitting inside the building: very high available fault current at its terminals, and dc has no zero crossing to help a device put out an arc. A breaker chosen by amp number alone can weld shut on dc fault current, leaving the circuit defended on paper only — inches from the largest energy source on the job.
inspection_fails: AC-rated breaker installed on the battery dc circuit — not listed for dc use (706.31(C)).
Overcurrent device sized at nameplate current with no 125% factor, and the assembly is not listed for 100% operation (706.31(B)).
Conductors sized to the nameplate current but smaller than the rating of the overcurrent device protecting them (706.30(B)).
DC fuse with an interrupting rating below the battery bank's available fault current.
sections.exam_trap: Two wrong answers live here. First: the battery breaker at exactly the 40 A nameplate current, because the inverter limits its output — 706.31(B) wants not less than 125% unless the assembly is listed for 100% operation. Second: an ac-rated breaker on the dc side because the amp number matched. On a battery circuit, the amp number is the least important thing on the device.

sections.title: Critical operations power systems (COPS)
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 708 covers power systems for facilities an AHJ or governmental authority has designated as critical operations areas — places like certain 911 and emergency operations centers, critical infrastructure and national-security functions, where losing power is a public-safety event, not an inconvenience. The article layers extra reliability, testing, documentation and risk-assessment duties on top of the standby ideas in Articles 700 to 702. Sharma's residential and light-commercial work will rarely be designated COPS, and the practical skill is recognizing the designation on the rare job that carries it.

sections.title: Stand-Alone systems — power with no utility to lean on
sections.plain_explanation: Article 710 covers systems that operate in island mode, not connected to a power production and distribution network: the off-grid house, the remote pump, the microgrid that runs alone. Because there is no utility behind the source, the article lets the supply be smaller than a normal calculated load — but never smaller than the realities on its own pages. Sources combine freely here (solar, storage, generator), and the same equipment often also appears under Articles 702, 705 and 706 when it works alongside a utility, so the first job is deciding which mode the system is actually in.
sections.on_the_job: Ask whether the utility exists on this job at all. 'No utility, ever' is 710; 'utility plus backup' is 702 or 705, and the sizing rules differ.

sections.title: Identification of power sources — stand-alone systems
sections.plain_explanation:
New in the 2020 code, 710.10 requires the power sources of a stand-alone system to be identified by a permanent plaque or directory. It is the same instinct as the 705.10 directory for interconnected sources: anyone working on or responding to the building can find every source and its disconnect.
• The plaque or directory is installed at the disconnecting means location, or another approved, readily visible location.
• It denotes the location of each power source disconnecting means serving the building.
• Where more than one source supplies the building, the marking carries the multiple-sources caution, the same as 705.10.
• A diagram on the plaque must be oriented the way the building actually sits.
On a system with solar, batteries and a generator scattered around a property, the identification is the difference between a safe shutdown and a scavenger hunt.
sections.on_the_job: On an off-grid house outside Ocala, the plaque at the house disconnect lists all three sources: the PV inverter disconnect and the battery disconnect on the garage west wall, and the generator disconnect in the detached shed. List every source on the identification, including the small generator that 'only feeds the barn.' If it can energize the wiring, it belongs on the list. Walk the property and verify each location before the plaque is made — a directory that points to where a disconnect was planned, instead of where it is, fails its only job.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A stand-alone system has no utility to call and no single service main to pull. Open the wrong disconnect and the building is still live from the battery inverter in the garage. The plaque is how a firefighter, a responder, or the next electrician finds every source before anyone touches the wiring.
inspection_fails: No plaque at all on an off-grid house — the inspector has to hunt for the battery and generator disconnects.
Plaque lists the PV and the battery but leaves off the generator in the detached shed.
Directory diagram drawn rotated from how the building actually sits, so the responder is sent to the wrong wall.
Hand-lettered paper label taped inside the panel instead of a permanent plaque (110.21(B)).
sections.exam_trap: The system is off-grid, so there is no service equipment, no utility — and, the trap answer says, no directory. Wrong. Section 710.10 was added in 2020 precisely for stand-alone systems, and it asks for the same thing 705.10 asks of interconnected systems. The second trap is citing 705.10 on a stand-alone job: the requirement is real, but on a 710 system it lives in 710.10.

sections.title: General rules — sizing a stand-alone supply
sections.plain_explanation: Premises wiring fed by a stand-alone system still has to meet the code the way a feeder- or service-fed installation does, with the modifications on this page. The supply may be smaller than the Article 220 calculated load, but the combined capacity of all the stand-alone sources must at least equal the load of the largest single piece of utilization equipment connected — general lighting load does not count as that single load. The 2020 code also expressly permits these systems to supply three-phase, three-wire or four-wire loads.
sections.on_the_job: Build the load list around the largest motor or appliance first, including its starting demand in the real-world conversation with the inverter maker. A system that cannot start its own well pump is undersized by this section's own test.

sections.title: Direct-current microgrids
sections.plain_explanation: Article 712, confirmed in the printed 2020 table of contents, covers dc microgrids: systems that distribute dc power from dc sources to dc loads, with converters tying them to ac systems where needed. It is a young article for a young technology, and Sharma's Florida work has not hit one yet. It earns its place in this book so the reader recognizes the article number and does not mistake a dc microgrid for an Article 710 stand-alone system or a 705 interconnection, which it can sit alongside.
sections.on_the_job: If a plan set shows a dc bus feeding loads, find this article before you assume the familiar ac rules answer everything.

sections.title: Directory — dc microgrid sources
sections.plain_explanation: This is Article 712's directory rule, the dc counterpart of 705.10 and 710.10: a permanent plaque or directory denoting all electric power sources on or in the premises, installed at each service equipment location and at the locations of power production sources capable of being interconnected, so anyone working the building can find every source and its disconnect. Subsection (B) covers the directory for a building supplied by a dc microgrid. Other articles send dc microgrid work here for its plaques and directories: battery systems under 480.7(G)(1), PV under 690.56(B), fuel cells under 692.4(B)(2) and wind systems under 694.54(B).
sections.on_the_job: Sharma has not installed a dc microgrid; this page is the signpost for the day one appears on a plan set. The field habit transfers directly from 705.10 work: directory at the service, every source named, disconnect locations shown.

sections.title: Circuits and equipment operating at less than 50 volts
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 720 is the small general article for circuits and equipment running under 50 volts, ac or dc, that are not claimed by a more specific article (720.1, 720.2). Most low-voltage work Sharma does is claimed: thermostats and controls by Article 725, fire alarm by 760, communications by Chapter 8. Article 720 is what remains — and what remains still has teeth:
• Conductors not smaller than 12 AWG copper or equivalent; on an appliance branch circuit supplying more than one appliance or appliance receptacle, not smaller than 10 AWG (720.4).
• Standard lampholders rated not less than 660 W (720.5), and receptacles rated not less than 15 A (720.6).
• Receptacles of not less than 20 A in kitchens, laundries, and other locations where portable appliances are likely to be used (720.7).
• Storage batteries follow the Article 480 rules named in 720.9, and the work is installed in a neat and workmanlike manner, cables supported so normal building use will not damage them (720.11).
sections.on_the_job: Name the owning article for every low-voltage run on the plan. On a shop remodel in Apopka, the crew found a legacy 32 V appliance circuit feeding three receptacles in a detached workshop. No specific article claims it, so Article 720 does: the run is rewired in 10 AWG copper — an appliance branch circuit with more than one receptacle — the receptacles are rated 15 A minimum, and 20 A receptacles go in at the bench where portable tools plug in. 'Low voltage' is a description, not a wiring method.

nec2023_change.change: Article 720 was deleted in the 2023 NEC — the Code panel found the equipment it covered had not been manufactured for decades and no known systems remain in service. Low-voltage work is governed by the specific articles that claim each circuit instead.
nec2023_change.source: Safer Buildings, 2023 NEC: 5 upcoming changes integrators need to know (Article 720 removed)

sections.why_it_exists: Fifty volts sits below the shock hazard that drives most of the Code, but not below the fire hazard. A low-voltage circuit on a stiff supply can push enough current to cook undersized conductors for hours. The minimum wire sizes and real receptacle ratings exist because low voltage tempts everyone to wire it like it cannot hurt anything.

sections.title: Article 722 — not in the 2020 code (a 2023 number)
sections.plain_explanation:
There is no Article 722 in NEC 2020. The number was first used in the 2023 edition, where a new Article 722 gathers the cable rules for power-limited circuits that the 2020 book spreads across Articles 725, 760 and 770. Florida work under the Florida Building Code 8th Edition (permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026) is NEC 2020, so a 2023 study book, app or exam sheet that sends you to 722 is pointing at a page this code does not have. In the 2020 book, the cable types, listing and substitution rules for Class 2 and Class 3 circuits live inside Article 725, the power-limited fire alarm cable rules live inside Article 760, and the optical fiber cable rules live in Article 770.

• Article 722: A new Article 722 was created for the general requirements for cables used with power-limited circuits and fault-managed power (Class 4) circuits installations.

Then flag the citation to the lead, because the rest of that document may be written to the wrong edition too.
