sections.title: Class 1, Class 2 and Class 3 circuits — controls and signaling
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 725 sorts remote-control, signaling and power-limited circuits into three classes, and the class comes from the power source, not from the wire in your hand. Class 1 circuits can carry serious energy and are wired much like power circuits. Class 2 circuits are limited so strictly that they are treated as safe from both shock and fire initiation — the thermostat, the doorbell, most controls. Class 3 circuits allow more voltage and power than Class 2, stay limited against fire, and need added protection against shock. The relaxed wiring methods in this article are earned by the listed power source; change the source and you may have changed the class.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 724/726: Article 725 was split: Class 1 power-limited circuits moved to new Article 724; Article 725 keeps Class 2 and Class 3; new Article 726 covers Class 4 fault-managed power systems; cable rules moved to new Article 722.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On every controls job, find the power source and read its label before you choose a cable. No listed Class 2 source, no Class 2 wiring methods.

sections.title: Definitions — what makes a circuit Class 2 or Class 3
sections.plain_explanation: The definitions draw the line this whole article stands on. A Class 2 circuit is the wiring between a Class 2 power source and its equipment, with power limited tightly enough that the circuit is considered safe against both electric shock and starting a fire. A Class 3 circuit is limited against fire initiation, but its voltage and power can still present a shock hazard, so added protection is part of the deal. A Class 1 circuit is everything in this family that is not power-limited that way, including remote-control and signaling circuits that can run up to 600 volts.
sections.on_the_job: When a helper asks why two identical-looking cables get treated differently, the answer is on the source label, and this definition is why.

sections.title: Power sources for Class 2 and Class 3 circuits
sections.plain_explanation: A Class 2 or Class 3 circuit has to be fed from a source this section recognizes: a listed Class 2 or Class 3 transformer, a listed Class 2 or Class 3 power supply, other listed equipment marked to identify it as the Class 2 or Class 3 source, or one of the other sources the section names, such as certain dry-cell battery supplies. A random wall-wart or an unmarked transformer does not create a Class 2 circuit, however small its output looks. The listing and the marking are the circuit's papers.
sections.on_the_job: Photograph the source label for the job record on controls work. At final inspection, that label is the fastest proof of what class the circuit is.

sections.title: Wiring methods on the load side of the source
sections.plain_explanation: On the load side of a Class 2 or Class 3 source, the wiring methods relax: the listed cable types for these circuits — the CL2 and CL3 families, power-limited tray cable and their permitted substitutions — may be installed without the raceways and boxes ordinary power wiring needs, following the application rules for the cable chosen. The supply side of the source is wired under the normal chapters; only the limited-energy side earns the relaxed methods. Cable choice still follows the building space it runs through, the way plenum and riser choices do elsewhere in the book.
sections.on_the_job: Keep the line straight in the field: full wiring methods up to the source, Class 2 or 3 cable methods after it. Blurring that line at the source is the most common controls rough-in mistake.

sections.title: Separation from power conductors — the general rule
sections.plain_explanation: Class 2 and Class 3 cables and conductors are not placed in the same cable, raceway, enclosure, box or similar fitting as electric light, power, Class 1, non-power-limited fire alarm or medium-power broadband conductors, unless one of the permissions in this section applies. The standing permissions are separation by a barrier, the tight rules for conductors that enter the same equipment, and the spacing rule for other applications on the next page. This section, and the 2-inch figure inside it, were re-checked against 2020 sources for this pass; the figure is real, but it belongs to one paragraph of this section, not to every low-voltage run.
sections.on_the_job: Default field rule: give Class 2 and 3 runs their own path. Then use the permissions on purpose, by name, when a shared box or a tight route is unavoidable.

sections.title: Other applications — the 2-inch spacing rule
sections.plain_explanation: For applications outside enclosures and equipment, Class 2 and Class 3 conductors are separated by at least 2 inches from conductors of electric light, power, Class 1, non-power-limited fire alarm and medium-power broadband circuits — unless one side or the other is in a raceway or in a metal-sheathed, metal-clad, nonmetallic-sheathed or Type UF cable, or the two are permanently separated by a suitable insulating barrier or tubing. The parallel rule for communications circuits lives in Chapter 8 at 800.133(A)(2), and it is also 2 inches, with its own raceway and cable exceptions. Two inches is a spacing for open runs, not a license to share a box, and not a number to apply where a barrier rule already governs.
sections.on_the_job: Carry the exceptions with the number: NM cable on the power side, or a raceway on either side, satisfies the condition without the open-air spacing. When neither side has that protection, hold the 2 inches along the run.

sections.title: Power and data in the same cable — 725.144 and PoE heating
sections.plain_explanation:
When a Class 2 cable carries power and data together — Power over Ethernet feeding cameras, access points, and lighting — every powered pair adds heat to the bundle, and a big bundle of powered cables runs hotter than the same bundle carrying data alone. 725.144 answers with ampacity limits for the conductors of Class 2 cables used to transmit power: the permitted current depends on the conductor size, the cable's temperature rating, and how many cables are bundled together. Type LP (limited power) cables carry their permitted ampacity in the cable marking, which takes the bundle question out of the table and puts it on the jacket. A cable that is fine for data is not automatically fine as a power-delivery cable in a full bundle.

Sharma's residential and light-commercial crews will meet it rarely, if ever, but the article sits between 725 and 728 in the printed book and the reader should know what the cable is when a commercial plan calls it out. sections.title: Fire-resistive cable systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 728 covers fire-resistive cable systems: listed systems, cable included, that are built and installed to keep critical circuits working through a rated period of fire exposure. These are the systems behind circuit-integrity cable on life-safety feeders — emergency feeders, fire pump feeders and critical operations circuits.
• The listing is a system, not just a cable. A system listed to UL 2196 (an FHIT system in the UL Fire Resistance Directory) names the exact cable, raceway, supports, splice kits and boxes, and the spacing of the supports.
• Install it exactly as the system listing describes, supports and all. A field substitution breaks the rating even when the cable itself looks identical.
• Where Article 728 and another article of the Code differ, Article 728 applies (728.3). The listing instructions are part of the installation, not paperwork.
• Listed systems carry a rated period — commonly 1 hour or 2 hours. The circuit being protected sets which rating the job needs.
sections.on_the_job: A 12-story condo on the Orlando corridor stands over 75 ft tall, so 700.10(D) requires 2-hour fire protection for its emergency feeders. Sharma runs the life-safety feeder as one listed 2-hour circuit-integrity system: cable, raceway, supports and splice kits all come from the single FHIT system on the approved submittal, and supports go at the spacing that system prints — not the spacing the crew usually uses. Photograph supports and terminations as you go; the rating lives in those details, and the inspector can ask for the FHIT document by number.

sections.why_it_exists: A fire does not wait for the panel schedule. The emergency feeder runs the exit lights, the fire alarm, the smoke control fans and the fire pump while people are still inside the building, and ordinary cable fails within minutes under direct flame. A fire-resistive system buys the rated time — up to 2 hours — for everyone to get out and for firefighters to work.
inspection_fails: Supports spaced by habit instead of at the spacing in the FHIT system listing — the system is not installed as listed (110.3(B)).
A substituted raceway or coupling that is not part of the listed system, so the 2-hour rating no longer exists.
A splice made with a standard kit where the system listing requires its own listed splice kit.
No FHIT system document on site for the inspector to check the installation against.
sections.exam_trap: The cable on the truck is the same circuit-integrity cable the last job used, so it gets hung on standard supports at the crew's usual spacing. That is the wrong answer. The rating belongs to the listed system — cable plus the raceway, supports and splices the FHIT document names. The same cable installed any other way is an unrated installation wearing a rated cable.

sections.title: Energy management systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 750 covers energy management systems: equipment that monitors and controls how a building uses energy, including the load-management systems that Articles 702 and 705 lean on when a generator or a panel is deliberately run below its unmanaged peak. The article's guardrail is that managing energy never means defeating safety: controls may shed, schedule and limit loads within their listings, and the overcurrent and disconnect rules of the rest of the book still stand behind them.

The EMS gets one current setpoint: the load used in the 220.70 calculation and the most current it allows on the supply it controls (750.30(C)(1)).
• 750.6: New in 2023: an energy management system (EMS) has to be listed, either as one complete system, as a kit installed in the field, or as listed components assembled into a system. Path 1: the EMS is listed as one complete system.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

sections.title: Fire alarm systems — wiring and power
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 760 covers the installation of wiring and equipment for fire alarm systems, including the circuits the fire alarm system controls and powers: detection, notification, sprinkler waterflow and supervisory signals, and functions like door release and elevator control that the alarm commands. System design, device placement and testing live in NFPA 72; this article governs how the wiring and power are installed. Every fire alarm circuit is one of two kinds — non-power-limited or power-limited — and the kind comes from its power source, exactly the way Article 725 classes come from theirs.

sections.title: Fire alarm circuit identification
sections.plain_explanation:
Fire alarm circuits are identified at terminal and junction locations, in a manner that helps prevent unintentional signals on the fire alarm circuits during testing and servicing of other systems.
• The identification lives where the work happens: at the terminals and at every junction location, not just on a panel schedule in the office.
• Alarm wiring that nobody can tell apart from everything else in a ceiling is an invitation to the next trade to disturb it.
• The manner of identification has to do its job — it must actually keep other work from putting false signals on the alarm circuits.
sections.on_the_job: On a tenant build-out in Altamonte Springs, the alarm circuits run through the same ceiling as the lighting and the HVAC controls. Identify as you terminate: every fire alarm circuit tagged at the panel terminals, and again at each junction box a later electrician might open — the box above the corridor, the splice over the stockroom. When the controls contractor comes back to test his system, he can see at a glance which conductors are not his. The identification is part of the install, not paperwork for the end of the job.

No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Fire alarm circuits share ceilings and junction boxes with power, lighting and low-voltage wiring. When a technician testing another system cannot tell which conductors are the alarm loop, a lifted lead or a stray jumper can put a false signal on the system — or silently take a detection circuit out of service. Identification at the points where hands actually touch the wiring is what keeps other work from becoming an alarm event.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer identifies the circuits only at the fire alarm control panel, or only on the drawings. 760.30 puts the identification at terminal and junction locations — the places where testing and service work actually opens the wiring. A panel schedule in the office does not stop a false signal in the ceiling.

sections.title: Circuit requirements — NPLFA follows Parts I and II, PLFA follows Parts I and III
sections.plain_explanation:
This short section is the traffic cop of Article 760: it tells you which parts of the article govern a circuit before you read any other rule.
• Non-power-limited fire alarm (NPLFA) circuits comply with Part I (general) and Part II (non-power-limited circuits).
• Power-limited fire alarm (PLFA) circuits comply with Part I (general) and Part III (power-limited circuits).
The circuit's family comes from its power source — 760.41 for NPLFA, 760.121 for PLFA — not from the wire on the truck. The two families allow different cables, different overcurrent protection, and different installation methods, so a rule read from the wrong part is a rule that does not apply: the classic Article 760 error.
sections.on_the_job: On a Winter Garden warehouse job, the drawings showed one fire alarm control unit fed from a dedicated branch circuit — an NPLFA system — and a second, smaller panel whose listed supply made its circuits power-limited. The apprentice priced one cable type for both. The foreman split the order: Parts I and II for the first system, Parts I and III for the second. Different cable, different protection, different separation rules — all of it decided by 760.35 before a single reel was cut.
sections.why_it_exists: The two families carry very different energy. An NPLFA circuit is fed like a power circuit and can deliver fault energy that starts fires; a PLFA source is limited, so its circuits cannot. Rules written for one energy level are wrong for the other: too lax for NPLFA, needlessly strict for PLFA. 760.35 exists so the installer sorts the circuit first and only then opens the rulebook.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer sends both families to the same parts — usually 'Part I and Part II for everything,' because Part II comes first in the article. PLFA circuits are governed by Parts I and III. If a question names a power-limited fire alarm circuit and an answer choice cites a Part II rule, it is wrong no matter how good the rule sounds.

sections.title: NPLFA circuit power source requirements
sections.plain_explanation: A non-power-limited fire alarm circuit is powered from a source that follows the normal wiring chapters, with output voltage not over 600 volts nominal. The branch circuit feeding the fire alarm equipment feeds nothing else, and the fire alarm circuit disconnect is allowed to be secured in the on position so a casual hand cannot silence the system's power. Section 760.41(B) adds the identification package: the overcurrent device is identified at the fire alarm control unit, the disconnecting means carries red identification marked FIRE ALARM CIRCUIT and is accessible only to qualified personnel, and the branch circuit is not supplied through ground-fault or arc-fault circuit-interrupter protection. NPLFA circuits carry real energy, which is why their conductors and protection are handled on the next pages like power wiring, not like bell wire.
sections.on_the_job: Dedicate the branch circuit and label it. If another load wants that circuit later, the answer is no, and this section is the reason you give.

sections.title: NPLFA overcurrent protection — small conductors, small limits
sections.plain_explanation:
Overcurrent protection for non-power-limited fire alarm (NPLFA) circuits is sized off the conductor, and the small conductors alarm work runs on get hard caps:
• 18 AWG conductors: overcurrent protection not over 7 A.
• 16 AWG conductors: overcurrent protection not over 10 A.
• Conductors 14 AWG and larger: protected in accordance with their ampacity.
The device is located where the conductor receives its supply, the way overcurrent protection normally works. Size the device to the smallest conductor on the run: a circuit that leaves the supply on 14 AWG and finishes on 18 AWG is protected as an 18 AWG circuit.
sections.on_the_job: On a strip-center fire alarm retrofit in Kissimmee, the notification runs leaving the power supplies were pulled in 18 AWG and 16 AWG, and the panel schedule showed the shop's standard 20 A breaker out of habit. The foreman caught it before trim: the 18 AWG legs went on protection not over 7 A and the 16 AWG legs not over 10 A, with each device at the point where its conductor receives supply, sized to the smallest conductor on the run, exactly as 760.43 requires.
sections.why_it_exists: A fault on an 18 AWG alarm conductor behind a 20 A breaker can cook the conductor's insulation long before the breaker notices: the wire becomes the fuse. Fire alarm circuits are also the last circuits that may ever fail silently, because a burned-open initiating circuit leaves a building with no alarm and no warning. Capping the protection at 7 A and 10 A keeps the small conductors from being the weak link in a life-safety system.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer sizes the device to the load: 'the horns only draw a few amps, so a 20 A breaker is fine.' 760.43 caps the device by conductor size, not by load: 7 A maximum on 18 AWG and 10 A maximum on 16 AWG, no matter how small the connected load is. When the question is about a fire alarm circuit, answer from Article 760, not from general breaker habit.

sections.title: Power sources for PLFA circuits — and the red breaker
sections.plain_explanation: A power-limited fire alarm circuit is fed from a listed PLFA transformer, a listed PLFA power supply, or listed equipment marked to identify its PLFA source — a fire alarm control panel with an integral source is the everyday example. The branch circuit behind that source feeds no other loads, its overcurrent device is identified in red, is accessible only to qualified personnel, and is marked as the fire alarm circuit, with the device identified at the fire alarm control unit. The red breaker is how the next electrician, and the building's own staff, learn in one glance which breaker must never be casually borrowed or switched. 760.121(B) imposes the same supply package as the non-power-limited rule in 760.41(B): the branch-circuit disconnecting means is identified in red and marked “FIRE ALARM CIRCUIT,” its location is identified at the fire alarm control unit, access is limited to qualified personnel — and the branch circuit must not be supplied through a ground-fault circuit-interrupter or arc-fault circuit-interrupter protective device.
sections.on_the_job: Use the red identification and the panel marking on every alarm job, and verify the branch circuit truly serves nothing else before you sign the panel schedule.

sections.title: Installation of PLFA cables in buildings
sections.plain_explanation: Power-limited fire alarm cables are installed by application: this section, working with the cable application and substitution tables later in the article, matches each listed cable type to where it may run — plenums, risers, trays, raceways and general building spaces. The method is table-driven on purpose: the cable's fire listing, not its color or its price, decides where it belongs. Circuit-integrity cable appears in this family where a design calls for circuits that must survive fire exposure, and it is installed as its listing directs.
sections.on_the_job: Read the cable jacket legend, find its row in the application table, then run it. Never decide a plenum or riser question from the cable's color.

sections.title: Optical fiber cables
sections.plain_explanation: Article 770, the last article of Chapter 7, covers the installation of optical fiber cables — glass or plastic fibers carrying light instead of current. Fiber cannot shock anyone or start a fire with its signal, so the article's real subjects are the cable's fire and smoke listing for the space it runs through, and what happens when fiber shares raceways and enclosures with conductors that do carry energy, especially conductive fiber cables with metallic strength members. Communications fiber also appears in Chapter 8's world; this article is fiber's home for installation rules.
sections.on_the_job: Treat a conductive fiber cable's metal member with the same respect as a conductor until you have confirmed how it is terminated and bonded. The light in the fiber is harmless; the metal around it is not automatically so.

sections.title: Installing optical fiber cables
sections.plain_explanation: 770.133 governs how optical fiber cables are installed with other systems. The dividing line is whether the fiber cable is conductive — carrying a metallic strength member, armor, or sheath — or nonconductive. Nonconductive fiber may share a raceway, enclosure, or cable tray with electric light, power, and Class 1 conductors under the conditions the section sets, because the fiber itself brings no conductive path into the box. Conductive fiber is treated with more suspicion: its metal member can carry a fault or a foreign potential into the enclosure, so the section restricts how it mixes with power conductors. Either way, the fiber cable's own listing for the space (770.179) still applies, and abandoned fiber comes out under the same discipline as the rest of Chapter 7.
sections.on_the_job: Pulling fiber toward a panel-adjacent raceway: the first question is conductive or nonconductive — read the jacket. Nonconductive dielectric fiber is the easy roommate; a steel-armored fiber changes the answer and gets its own path.
sections.figure_idea: Two raceway cross-sections: nonconductive fiber sharing with power; conductive fiber separated.

sections.title: Optical fiber cable types — reading the letters
sections.plain_explanation: The type letters on an optical fiber cable tell you two things: whether the cable is conductive, and where its fire and smoke listing lets it run. OFN is optical fiber nonconductive; OFC is optical fiber conductive — the C means a metallic member is part of the cable. The suffix grades the listing like the communications ladder in Chapter 8: OFNP and OFCP are plenum grade, OFNR and OFCR are riser grade, and plain OFN and OFC are general purpose. A higher grade may substitute for a lower one; a lower grade never substitutes up. Match the letters to the space — plenum, riser, or general — the same way you match CMP, CMR, and CM. OFNG/OFCG and OFN/OFC are general-purpose grade. A nonconductive type may substitute for the conductive type of the same or lower grade (e.g., OFNR for OFCR), but a conductive type never substitutes for a nonconductive one.
sections.on_the_job: Spec says OFNR for a riser shaft and the truck has OFN: that pull does not happen. Plenum-rated fiber (OFNP or OFCP) in the truck covers the riser too — the ladder only runs downhill.
